Group differences in OXT methylation between patients with Major Depressive Disorder and healthy controls: A pre-registered replication study
Simon Sanwald, Christian Montag, Markus Kiefer

ABSTRACT
Depression is linked to stress which leaves traces in the epigenetic signature of genes. The oxytocin system is implicated in allostatic processes promoting adaption to environmental stressors. Interactions of the oxytocin system with the environment, e.g., methylation of the gene coding for oxytocin (OXT), are candidates for the investigation of the biological underpinnings of depression. Recently, we found hypomethylation of OXT in patients with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) compared to healthy controls (HC). Since the replicability of findings is a key point of criticism in (epi‑)genetic research, we aimed to confirm our previous findings in a pre-registered study (data was stored in a database prior to pre-registration) within a new sample of n = 85 patients with MDD and n = 85 HC. decisions.reason: The 2024 abstract (n = 85 MDD, n = 85 HC) retests and confirms "our previous findings" / "our previous study" showing OXT hypomethylation in MDD patients compared to healthy controls, alongside stressful life events (SLEs) and depression severity. In the complete deposited bibliography (bib0001-bib0058), bib0043 (10.1186/s12888-021-03166-6) studies SLC6A4, leaving two 2020 Sanwald et al. OXT methylation papers: bib0042 (J. Affect. Disord., 10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.068, shipped row 821) and bib0041 (J. Mol. Neurosci., 10.1007/s12031-019-01446-1). In the verified primary abstracts, abstract_03 (10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.068) explicitly reports a case-control study of 90 MDD inpatients and 90 matched HCs with significantly lower OXT promoter methylation in MDD vs. HC, plus SLE and depression-severity analyses. By contrast, abstract_04 (10.1007/s12031-019-01446-1) reports N = 146 MDD inpatients examining SLEs, depression severity, and sex differences, with no HC group in its title or abstract. Although the 2024 body/in-text citations and both 2020 full bodies remain inaccessible (so unreported body contrasts in bib0041 are not assumed impossible from title/abstract alone), under Codebook Step 2 only bib0042 positively states the retested MDD-vs.-HC OXT hypomethylation finding; hypothetical unseen body analyses in bib0041 do not make two references fit equally well. Target 0 therefore binds by description to shipped row 821 and is already represented.

Academic and behavior combined support: A single-case practice-based replication study.
Gettinger M, Kratochwill TR, Levin JR, Eubanks A, Foy A.

The purpose of this research was to conduct a practice-based replication of Academic and Behavior Combined Support (ABC Support), a previously developed and experimentally evaluated supplemental intervention that merges a combined focus on reading fluency and academic engagement. In the present study, a school-based interventionist and data collector had access to implementation resources online and participated in virtual training and coaching. Four Grade 2 students received the ABC Support intervention for 6 weeks in their school. Students' oral fluency on training and non-training reading passages, as well as occurrence of engagement and disruptive behaviors during universal reading instruction, were measured repeatedly across baseline, intervention, and follow-up phases in a multiple-baseline design. decisions.reason: The 2024 abstract reports a 4-student Grade 2 multiple-baseline practice-based replication of Academic and Behavior Combined Support (ABC Support), "a previously developed and experimentally evaluated supplemental intervention," finding baseline-to-intervention and follow-up gains in reading fluency and classroom behavior "[i]n concert with prior empirical findings on ABC Support." Across the 49 deposited references (bb0005-bb0245), only two entries concern ABC Support: bb0085 (Gettinger, Kratochwill, Eubanks, Foy, & Levin, 2021, J. Sch. Psychol. 89, 1-19, 10.1016/j.jsp.2021.09.004, shipped row 1563) and bb0090 (Gettinger, Kratochwill, Foy, & Eubanks, 2021 online / 2022 print, Intervention in School and Clinic 58(1), 15-20, 10.1177/10534512211047571). Inspection of both complete primary texts establishes that 10.1016/j.jsp.2021.09.004 (09_gettinger_evaluation.unrepaired.txt) is the sole prior experimental evaluation of ABC Support, testing six Grade 2 teacher-student dyads in a randomized multiple-baseline design and reporting significant gains in standard-passage WCPM (p = .006), training-passage WCPM (p = .001), academic engagement (p = .001), and reduced disruptive behavior (p = .001). Conversely, 10.1177/10534512211047571 (10_gettinger_development.unrepaired.txt) is practitioner implementation guidance (10 elements and 15 steps) with no empirical sample, design, or outcome analysis. While 2024 in-text citation attribution remains unavailable without the 2024 body, Codebook Step 2 uniquely binds target 0 by description to the empirical evaluation in shipped row 1563.

Virtual reality assessment of a high-calorie food bias: Replication and food-specificity in healthy participants
Philipp Alexander Schroeder, Enrico Collantoni, Johannes Lohmann, Martin V. Butz, Christian Plewnia

BACKGROUND: Theoretical models and behavioural studies indicate faster approach behaviour for high-calorie food (approach bias) among healthy participants. A previous study with Virtual Reality (VR) and online motion-capture quantified this approach bias towards food and non-food cues in a controlled VR environment with hand movements. The aim of this study was to test the specificity of a manual approach bias for high-calorie food in grasp movements compared to low-calorie food and neutral objects of different complexity, namely, simple balls and geometrically more complex office tools. METHODS: In a VR setting, healthy participants (N = 27) repeatedly grasped or pushed high-calorie food, low-calorie food, balls and office tools in randomized order with 30 item repetitions. decisions.reason: The 2024 abstract (N = 27 healthy participants grasping or pushing high-calorie food, low-calorie food, balls, and office tools in VR) states that "[a] previous study with Virtual Reality (VR) and online motion-capture quantified this approach bias towards food and non-food cues in a controlled VR environment with hand movements" and finds faster grasp and collection for high-calorie food. In the deposited bibliography (bib1-bib73), two primary VR + Leap Motion hand-movement studies in healthy adults from the same group are candidate originals: (1) bib60, Schroeder, Lohmann, Butz, & Plewnia (2016, Cyberpsychol. Behav. Soc. Netw. 19(2), 120-126, 10.1089/cyber.2015.0311, shipped row 1827; complete accepted manuscript in 19_lohmann_thesis.unrepaired.txt), which tested 23 recruited / 20 analyzed healthy participants grasping/warding high-calorie food vs. balls and found faster food movement onset/contact and faster food collection (p = .002); and (2) bib39, Max, Schroeder, Blechert, Giel, Ehlis, & Plewnia (2021, Brain Struct. Funct. 226(4), 1169-1183, 10.1007/s00429-021-02232-9; complete text in 02_max_fulltext.all_text.unrepaired.txt), an explicit follow-up (33 recruited / 30 analyzed) adding office-tool complexity controls and fNIRS in a VR/touchscreen category-selection task, finding faster food movement onset (p < .001) but slower VR food collection (p < .001) in explicit contrast to Schroeder et al. (2016). Although 2024 grasp/collect results align more closely with 2016 while adopting 2021's office-tool control, task differences alone do not exclude a follow-up from the replication chain, and without the inaccessible 2024 body/in-text citations it remains undeterminable whether target 0 binds to row 1827 alone, bib39, or both.
